title: Neanderthal Woodworking Was Far More Advanced Than Previously Believed, Study Reveals
body:
The discovery of nearly six hundred wooden artefacts at the Abric Romaní rock‑shelter in Catalonia has forced scientists to rewrite the narrative of Neanderthal technology. The finds, dated to between 62,000 and 40,000 years ago, demonstrate that these hominins were not merely opportunistic fire‑users but skilled woodworkers who fashioned spears, structural supports and a variety of tools. The breadth and sophistication of the assemblage suggest that Neanderthals possessed a nuanced understanding of timber selection, shaping techniques and functional design far beyond what was previously assumed.

The artefacts, recovered over a decade of meticulous excavation, include long, tapered points that match the dimensions of hafted spears, as well as shorter, finely carved implements that appear to have served as scrapers, wedges and even components of shelter frames. Imprints of wooden beams and postholes in the sediment indicate that the shelter itself was reinforced with timber, implying a deliberate effort to modify the natural environment for comfort and protection. Microscopic analysis of the surfaces reveals cut marks consistent with stone tools, confirming that Neanderthals deliberately shaped the wood rather than merely collecting driftwood or charred remains.

These results challenge the long‑standing view that Neanderthal material culture was limited to stone, bone and occasional fire‑altered wood. Previous research had identified charred fragments in hearths, but the new evidence shows purposeful woodworking that required planning, skill and knowledge of wood properties such as flexibility, strength and resistance to decay. The selection of specific tree species—primarily conifers with straight trunks—suggests an early form of resource management, while the presence of both utilitarian and possibly symbolic items hints at a cultural complexity that rivals that of contemporary Homo sapiens.

The implications extend beyond Neanderthal craftsmanship. By demonstrating that timber was an integral part of their subsistence strategies, the study reshapes our understanding of how these groups exploited their ecosystems. Wooden spears would have expanded hunting ranges and increased success rates, while constructed shelters could have facilitated longer occupations in marginal climates. Moreover, the ability to produce a range of wooden tools may have reduced reliance on lithic raw material, allowing Neanderthals to adapt to regions where high‑quality stone was scarce.

Scholars caution that the Abric Romaní site may represent a regional specialty rather than a universal Neanderthal practice. Yet the sheer volume of artefacts and the diversity of functions provide a compelling case that woodworking was a widespread, perhaps essential, component of Neanderthal lifeways. Future investigations at other sites, coupled with experimental archaeology that replicates the techniques observed, will be crucial to determine how far this knowledge spread across the species’ range.

As the picture of Neanderthal ingenuity sharpens, the boundary between them and modern humans grows increasingly porous. The Abric Romaní findings underscore that the capacity for sophisticated toolmaking and environmental modification was not exclusive to Homo sapiens. Continued interdisciplinary research promises to reveal further layers of Neanderthal ingenuity, potentially reshaping the story of human evolution and the shared roots of technological innovation.
